title: Tiered SLOs + Error Budgets Kickoff (Hosted vs Dedicated)
topics: SLO table scope: chat/completions streaming, non-streaming, embeddings, model catalog ops
Streaming disconnect taxonomy (client abort vs server fault)
Latency SLIs for streaming (TTFT vs end-to-end)
Error budget burn-rate alerting and enforcement (release gates, canary-only, mitigation)
summary: Cross-functional kickoff to align on tiered SLO definitions and an error budget policy that will be enforced via rollout gates and runtime/routing mitigations. The group aligned on principles (Dedicated should be narrower and more predictable; Hosted should be multi-tenant and broader), the initial SLI set (availability/success, 5xx+timeouts, streaming disconnect rate, p95/p99 latency with TTFT for streaming, embeddings latency/error, model catalog ops), and the need to add a Dedicated-specific pool readiness indicator. Open questions were captured around how to attribute streaming disconnects, what constitutes "customer-side" timeout, and how to keep tier/region/model/route dimensions within cardinality budget. Owners were assigned for SLO draft tables, SLI spec, burn-rate alerting, and the first warn-only release gate pilot.
action_items: Aisha Bello: Draft Hosted tier SLO strawman (SLIs + targets + exclusions) for chat/completions (streaming + non-streaming) and embeddings; share in Confluence by 2026-01-22.
Lauren Bishop: Provide Dedicated customer expectation inputs (current commitments, common escalations) and confirm whether pool readiness should be page-worthy vs ticket-only; due 2026-01-22.
Vanessa Ortiz (via Priya Natarajan): Propose Dedicated pool readiness measurement options (scheduler health, capacity signal, provision-to-ready time) and where it is emitted; due 2026-01-24.
Amara Diallo: Inventory current gateway metrics for streaming disconnects and 499/timeout classification; list gaps and propose logging changes; due 2026-01-23.
Logan Wright + Nadia Rahman: Review label/cardinality impact for tier/region/model/route breakdowns; propose aggregation/sampling strategy; due 2026-01-27.
Sergio Costa: Sketch SLO dashboard template + naming conventions and required filters/links; due 2026-01-29.
Connor O'Brien: Outline change management policy hooks for "budget at risk" vs "budget exhausted" (warn-only, soft block, hard block) and exception criteria; due 2026-01-30.
Jordan Lee + Ethan Park: Identify the minimal budget-check API shape needed for CI/deploy gate and canary analysis (inputs/outputs, scope rules); due 2026-01-28.
Talia Benson: Send a 3-phase timeline proposal with milestones and owners; schedule weekly 30-min working sync; due 2026-01-16.
next_steps: Publish kickoff notes and owner list in the eng-sre Confluence space.
Schedule a focused follow-up on streaming SLIs (disconnects + TTFT) with Gateway + Runtime metrics owners.
Hold a target-setting session once the historical benchmark extract is validated (backtest suggested targets vs Q4/Q1 data).
Start with a small warn-only gate pilot (API gateway + routing) before expanding enforcement to more services.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Tiered SLOs + Error Budgets Kickoff (Hosted vs Dedicated)
Date: Jan 15, 2026 3:42 PM PST
Duration: 52 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Sean Gallagher (SRE Director)
- Rafael Mendes (SRE Manager)
- Aisha Bello (SRE)
- Priya Natarajan (VP Eng, Platform)
- Ethan Park (EM, Control Plane)
- Mina Haddad (EM, Smart Routing)
- Ravi Menon (Staff, Routing)
- Jordan Lee (Policy Engine)
- Lauren Bishop (Dir PM, Dedicated)
- Marissa Cole (Dir PM, Console & Rollouts)
- Paula Mendes (SPM, Rollouts)
- Logan Wright (Telemetry)
- Nadia Rahman (Metering / SLI data correctness)
- Sergio Costa (Dashboards / Alerting)
- Connor O'Brien (Release governance)
- Talia Benson (Program Mgmt)
- Amara Diallo (API Gateway)


[00:00] Sean Gallagher: Alright, I think we’re live. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the kickoff for tiered SLO definitions plus error budget policy and the enforcement mechanisms. The intent is we stop treating SLOs as a doc and start treating them as a control system, right.

[00:18] Sean Gallagher: Two outcomes from today: one, align on tier principles and scope, like what journeys we’re measuring and what we’re not. Two, agree on owners and timeline so we can ship this in phases. Rafael’s got a doc open but we’ll capture in notes.

[00:33] Rafael Mendes: Yeah and just to level set, the last quarter we had multiple incidents where we learned after the fact that we burned budget, but nobody felt it until customers were already escalated. The idea is make burn visible and tied to changes.

[00:49] Priya Natarajan: And from platform side, we want to make sure whatever we define is implementable and doesn’t explode metrics cost. Like per model, per route, per region is… a lot.

[01:01] Sean Gallagher: Exactly. So first: tier principles. I’ll propose something and people can poke holes. Hosted tier is multi-tenant, broad model catalog, and it’s okay that we have more variance. Dedicated tier is isolation and predictable throughput—so the SLO should be tighter but also scoped to what we actually control in the pool.

[01:21] Lauren Bishop: Plus Dedicated expectations are like, customers think they bought “their cluster” even if it’s our managed pool. If we don’t define readiness and capacity behavior, we get tickets that aren’t exactly 5xx but “you weren’t ready” or autoscaling took 20 minutes.

[01:38] Aisha Bello: Right, so for Dedicated we probably need a “pool readiness” SLI, not just request success rate. Like, can the pool accept traffic at the committed baseline.

[01:49] Ethan Park: That’s going to require a canonical definition. Otherwise it becomes a bunch of ad hoc “is scheduler healthy” signals.

[02:00] Mina Haddad: Also routing will need to know what to do when budget is burning. Hosted can fall back to compatible models or other regions. Dedicated is trickier: fallback might violate isolation or customer pinning.

[02:14] Sean Gallagher: Good. So scope: SLIs per tier for key journeys. I’m thinking:
- Chat/completions non-streaming: success rate and p95/p99 latency.
- Chat/completions streaming: success rate, time-to-first-token, and streaming disconnect rate.
- Embeddings: success and latency.
- Model catalog/control plane operations: list models, resolve model version, maybe “create deployment” for Dedicated.
- Dedicated readiness: pool ready and maybe provision-to-ready time.

[02:44] Marissa Cole: For Console we can surface those budgets, but we need consistent dimensions. Tier, region, model, route. And then some notion of service owner.

[02:56] Paula Mendes: And for rollouts, we need a clear answer to “when do we block canary promotion.” Like, budget at risk vs exhausted.

[03:06] Connor O'Brien: Yeah. From change management perspective, we can’t jump straight to hard blocks across everything. We probably do warn-only, then soft block in pilot, then hard block for a small set of services.

[03:20] Sean Gallagher: Agree. The enforcement is a phase 2 thing. Phase 0/1 is definitions and dashboards.

[03:29] Rafael Mendes: Maybe we should define “at risk” as a burn-rate threshold, multi-window. Like 2% budget burned in an hour and trending, versus “exhausted” when remaining is below X.

[03:42] Logan Wright: Multi-window burn is the standard approach. The tricky part is the SLIs have to be correct or you page the org on bad math.

[03:51] Nadia Rahman: And the tricky part is classification. Like what counts as failure. 499 vs 5xx, gateway timeouts vs customer timeouts, streaming disconnects. We saw last month we were counting client aborts as server faults in one path.

[04:08] Amara Diallo: Yeah, on gateway we have 499 but it’s not always client abort. Sometimes it’s upstream closing and we bubble it weirdly. The log line is not consistent between streaming and non streaming.

[04:22] Sean Gallagher: Great segue. Streaming SLIs are the spiciest. Let’s park “streaming disconnect taxonomy” as a dedicated follow-up, but we need an initial stance for the SLO table.

[04:35] Aisha Bello: For hosted streaming, I propose we track:
- TTFT p95/p99
- Stream completion success rate (received [DONE] or normal end)
- Disconnect rate, with categories: client aborted, server aborted, network.
And for SLO, we might exclude client aborted from availability.

[04:55] Mina Haddad: But customers don’t always accept “exclude client abort” because from their perspective it’s still a bad experience.

[05:04] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated customers especially will say “we didn’t abort.” They’ll claim the SDK retried because of our latency.

[05:12] Priya Natarajan: This is why we need definitions that are defensible and also measureable. If we exclude too much we’re just gaming it.

[05:21] Sean Gallagher: Yep. The exclusion list needs to be explicit: invalid auth, bad requests, customer mis-use, customer side timeouts if we can detect them, etc. But we can’t hide systemic issues behind exclusions.

[05:36] Sergio Costa: On dashboards, we can show the raw metrics plus the “SLO-measured” version. Like two lines. That helps with trust.

[05:44] Rafael Mendes: Also we need to decide measurement windows. Most SLOs will be 28-day rolling. But for enforcement we’ll look at burn over 1h/6h windows.

[05:56] Sean Gallagher: Right. Ok let’s talk tier principles more concretely.

[06:03] Sean Gallagher: Hosted: We’ll define SLOs for our top endpoints and apply across regions, but maybe allow some model variance. Dedicated: SLO is per customer pool, per region, pinned model version(s). We should not average across customers.

[06:22] Jordan Lee: That has implications for policy engine. The “scope” key needs to include tier, and for Dedicated probably an account or deployment id. But then metrics cardinality gets gnarly.

[06:34] Logan Wright: Exactly. We can’t label every metric with account_id. We can compute per-customer SLOs in a separate pipeline that reads logs with access controls.

[06:46] Nadia Rahman: Or we do “Dedicated SLO views” as derived metrics stored in restricted datasets, not in general Prom metrics.

[06:56] Marissa Cole: For Console we’ll need a permissions model. Like only that customer’s operator view can see their pool readiness and their budgets.

[07:06] Priya Natarajan: That’s probably phase 3. For now, internal enforcement can work on service/tier scope, not per customer.

[07:15] Lauren Bishop: I’m okay with that initially, but the Dedicated story can’t be “we have a tier but we can’t measure it.” We at least need pool readiness and request SLIs per pool internally.

[07:29] Sean Gallagher: I think we can. We just need to do it in a safe way.

[07:35] Talia Benson: Can I jump in on timeline? I heard phases. What are we targeting for phase 0 and 1? Like weeks.

[07:44] Sean Gallagher: Tentative. Phase 0: two to three weeks baseline + draft. Phase 1: four to six weeks to publish SLO definitions, implement SLI calculations, dashboards, and burn alerts. Phase 2: four to eight weeks enforcement via release gates and routing mitigations.

[08:04] Talia Benson: Great, I’ll put that into a plan and schedule weekly working sessions.

[08:10] Ethan Park: For control plane, we need to understand what the “budget check API” looks like. Is it “service X in tier Y is in red, block deploy”? Or do we do “route scope” like /v1/chat/completions.

[08:24] Aisha Bello: I think service-level for initial gating. Route-level later.

[08:30] Paula Mendes: For rollouts it’s usually “the thing you’re rolling out,” like a service or a deployment target. Route-level is hard.

[08:39] Mina Haddad: Also for routing mitigations, we need signal at route/model level. Like if a specific model variant is burning budget due to KV cache bug, we want to steer away from it.

[08:52] Ravi Menon: But if you do that, you need to define “compatible fallback.” That’s a product decision too. Like is falling back from Model A to Model B allowed in Hosted always? Or only when error rates spike.

[09:06] Marissa Cole: Product-wise, we should document what “graceful degradation” means per tier. Hosted: can fall back to a compatible model family with a banner in console maybe. Dedicated: fallbacks are opt-in via policy.

[09:20] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated fallbacks need to respect contract and customer expectations. Some will accept fallback, some won’t.

[09:28] Jordan Lee: That implies the policy engine needs a customer config flag for fallback behavior. But again, maybe phase 2/3.

[09:37] Sean Gallagher: Right now, for kickoff, let’s keep focus: define SLOs and error budget policy, plus initial enforcement hooks. We can make “fallback policy” an appendix with defaults.

[09:51] Rafael Mendes: Can we talk about targets? Like 99.9 vs 99.95, etc.

[09:56] Sean Gallagher: We’re not setting final numbers today. We’ll propose based on historical. But we should agree on the method: pick targets that are achievable with investment, not wishful.

[10:09] Aisha Bello: I’ll take the action to draft strawman targets for Hosted based on the last 90 days, but I want Nadia to sanity check SLI correctness.

[10:19] Nadia Rahman: Yeah, and we should compare log-based ground truth versus metrics. Especially for streaming.

[10:28] Amara Diallo: We’ll need to fix gateway instrumentation anyway. The current “stream end” event is not always emitted.

[10:37] Sean Gallagher: Ok, streaming disconnect taxonomy: what are the categories we can detect.

[10:44] Amara Diallo: Off the top: client closed connection, upstream closed, gateway timeout, and unknown. But distinguishing upstream closed vs network is hard.

[10:54] Ravi Menon: If runtime stops emitting tokens due to OOM or watchdog, it might look like upstream closed.

[11:03] Priya Natarajan: And if it’s a mobile network flake, it’s client closed but not their intent.

[11:10] Aisha Bello: We could define “server-attributable disconnect” as cases where we see a server-side error or timeout before disconnect, or we never sent first token.

[11:22] Mina Haddad: For routing, TTFT is important. If TTFT blows up, customers cancel. That shows up as client abort.

[11:31] Sean Gallagher: Great point. So if TTFT is bad, client aborts rise, and we can’t just exclude them blindly. We need a combined view.

[11:41] Sergio Costa: We can chart TTFT and client abort rate together. And for SLO we can treat “no first token within X seconds” as a timeout, regardless of who hung up.

[11:53] Rafael Mendes: That’s basically reclassifying the experience: if we didn’t respond in time, it’s on us.

[12:01] Ethan Park: But then we need consistent timeout thresholds across SDK, gateway, and internal timeouts.

[12:08] Nadia Rahman: And document it. Like “server timeout is 60 seconds to first token” or whatever. Otherwise everyone argues after the fact.

[12:18] Sean Gallagher: Ok. This is already enough for a follow-up meeting.

[12:23] Sean Gallagher: Dedicated pool readiness: Lauren, can you explain the pain from customers.

[12:30] Lauren Bishop: Sure. We get escalations like “your dedicated endpoint is up but p99 is 20 seconds,” or “after a scale event, we saw 10 minutes of slow responses,” or “we got capacity errors.” Sometimes it’s autoscaling lag, sometimes it’s GPU health, sometimes it’s scheduling. Customers want a single answer: are you ready to serve.

[12:53] Lauren Bishop: So I’d like a readiness SLI: percentage of time pool has at least N healthy replicas / capacity units and scheduler is green. And then maybe “time to ready” when we do changes.

[13:07] Priya Natarajan: We can probably measure that from the scheduler and capacity manager. Vanessa owns some of those signals.

[13:16] Ethan Park: But we need to define whether readiness is an SLO or a separate internal indicator. SLOs are customer-visible by definition.

[13:25] Sean Gallagher: Not necessarily publicly visible, but they should map to customer expectations. For Dedicated, readiness can be part of what we show in Console eventually.

[13:36] Marissa Cole: For MVP, we can show “Dedicated pool readiness” as a panel but maybe not expose as an external SLA-ish number. Yet.

[13:45] Connor O'Brien: Also, if readiness dips, do we page? We’ll page ourselves to death if autoscaling causes brief dips.

[13:54] Rafael Mendes: That’s where burn-rate and alerting sensitivity matters. We can have ticket-only for mild dips, page when burn suggests customer impact.

[14:06] Sean Gallagher: Good. Let’s switch to enforcement. What happens when budgets are at risk.

[14:13] Connor O'Brien: Proposal: three states.
1) Healthy: normal change velocity.
2) At risk: warn-only gate, extra canary scrutiny, require SRE approval for risky changes.
3) Exhausted: soft freeze on non-incident changes, canary-only deployments, only bug fixes with explicit approval.
Hard blocks only for a pilot, and we have override tokens with audit trail.

[14:42] Paula Mendes: For rollouts, we can implement “budget exhausted blocks promotion” and show “blocked due to error budget” in UI. The override flow needs to be explicit and time-bounded.

[14:56] Jordan Lee: Policy engine can enforce “only allow override if approver is in group SRE-leads” and TTL is <= 24 hours.

[15:06] Ethan Park: Control plane can provide the endpoint to query budget status and accept override tokens. That’s doable.

[15:14] Mina Haddad: Routing mitigations: if burn spikes, we can do protective throttling on Hosted, or failover to region B. But that needs to not create cascading overload.

[15:28] Ravi Menon: And for model fallback, we should define constraints. Like only within the same family, only if customer didn’t pin, only if the fallback is in “verified” set.

[15:41] Sean Gallagher: That’s good. We’ll write it into the mitigation playbook. But again, not all day today.

[15:49] Logan Wright: Just calling out: any of this needs accurate SLIs. If the SLI is wrong, gates block and people will disable the system.

[15:58] Nadia Rahman: +1. And we need to control cardinality. If we add model label + route label + region label + tier label, we’re okay. If we add account id, we’re dead.

[16:10] Priya Natarajan: So we agree: no account_id labels in general metrics.

[16:15] Lauren Bishop: But we still need per-customer Dedicated SLOs.

[16:19] Logan Wright: That can be derived in a separate restricted pipeline. Not Prom. That’s a separate design.

[16:26] Sergio Costa: On dashboards, we can start with tier + region + route + model for Hosted, and for Dedicated start with tier + pool id but only in restricted dashboards.

[16:38] Marissa Cole: And that aligns with Console permissions later.

[16:42] Sean Gallagher: Good. Let’s talk about what is excluded. I want to avoid repeating last year’s debate.

[16:50] Aisha Bello: Exclusions list draft:
- 4xx due to invalid auth, invalid params, rate limit (429) might be excluded from availability but tracked separately.
- Requests that never reached gateway (customer-side network) excluded.
- Customer-requested cancellations maybe excluded, but only if TTFT was within threshold.
- Abuse / policy blocked requests.

[17:14] Amara Diallo: For 429, we need to decide. If we do “protective throttling,” that’s us returning 429 deliberately. Does that count against SLO.

[17:24] Sean Gallagher: That’s a policy choice. My leaning: protective throttling should not count as success, but it may be excluded from availability if it’s explicitly a mitigation and we communicate it. However, we should track it and it will show up in customer experience.

[17:43] Marissa Cole: For status page, if we’re protective throttling materially, we probably post an incident anyway.

[17:50] Rafael Mendes: Also, “capacity errors” in Dedicated should count against readiness and maybe availability.

[17:59] Lauren Bishop: Yes. If we sold baseline throughput, then capacity errors are on us.

[18:06] Priya Natarajan: Unless customer exceeded agreed RPS. But that’s metering.

[18:12] Nadia Rahman: We can separate “over quota” vs “no capacity.” But it requires consistent error codes.

[18:21] Ethan Park: Control plane returns a specific error when deployment is out of capacity. We can map that.

[18:28] Sean Gallagher: Great. Ok, I want to make sure we leave with clear owners.

[18:34] Sean Gallagher: Aisha, you own the SLO definitions draft, Hosted first. Rafael will review. Lauren, you’ll provide Dedicated expectations and help shape Dedicated SLO table. Priya will loop in Vanessa for readiness signals. Amara and Nadia will drive streaming disconnect measurement. Logan and Nadia for correctness and cardinality. Sergio for dashboards. Connor for enforcement policy with Paula and Marissa for rollout integration.

[19:03] Talia Benson: I’ll capture that and send out notes today, and schedule weekly.

[19:10] Paula Mendes: Can we also decide where the source of truth lives. Confluence page with table plus a schema in repo.

[19:19] Jordan Lee: We should have both. Human-readable doc and a machine-readable config for gates and dashboards.

[19:27] Ethan Park: If we have a config, it needs validation. Like required fields: tier, service, SLI definition, target, window, exclusions.

[19:39] Priya Natarajan: And it needs to be stable. We can’t break older tenants.

[19:44] Sean Gallagher: That’s an ADR. We’ll do it.

[19:49] Sergio Costa: For dashboards, a consistent naming convention: SLO - <tier> - <region> - <service> - <route group>. And links to runbooks.

[20:00] Rafael Mendes: Also, burn-rate alert standard: multi-window 1h/6h or 5m/1h depending tier. Hosted is noisier.

[20:12] Sean Gallagher: Yep. Hosted alerts probably go to platform oncall; Dedicated to dedicated oncall. We’ll align later.

[20:22] Mina Haddad: Question: do we include latency SLO in error budget, or separate.

[20:28] Aisha Bello: I propose availability and latency both have their own budgets. But enforcement initially might be on availability burn only.

[20:37] Connor O'Brien: For change freeze, availability makes sense. Latency is important but we need to avoid blocking for minor regressions.

[20:45] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated customers care about p99 latency a lot though.

[20:50] Priya Natarajan: Maybe “latency burn” triggers at-risk state but not full exhaustion gates initially.

[20:58] Sean Gallagher: That sounds right: have latency SLO, monitor, alert, but gate on availability first.

[21:07] Marissa Cole: From UX side, in Console we can show both budgets. But gating UI might show “blocked due to availability budget.”

[21:16] Ravi Menon: For routing mitigations, latency burn can still trigger failover or reduce max tokens, like degrade quality to preserve latency.

[21:28] Sean Gallagher: That’s a policy question. We might do “protective measures” on Hosted when latency spikes. Dedicated probably shouldn’t change semantics unless customer opts in.

[21:41] Ethan Park: Ok. One more thing: measurement boundaries. Gateway vs runtime. For latency, do we measure end-to-end at gateway.

[21:49] Nadia Rahman: Ideally gateway, because it captures user-perceived. But we should also have component latency in traces.

[21:57] Amara Diallo: Gateway can measure request duration for non-streaming, and TTFT for streaming if we instrument it properly.

[22:06] Mina Haddad: But for streaming, end-to-end duration is weird because some customers stream for a long time.

[22:11] Aisha Bello: Exactly. For streaming, we should do TTFT and maybe tokens/sec distribution, but not total duration as an SLO. Or we cap the considered duration.

[22:24] Sean Gallagher: Great. Ok, we’ll write that down as “latency SLI for streaming is TTFT; non-streaming is full duration.”

[22:33] Sergio Costa: We can add “stream throughput” as a diagnostic panel, not an SLO.

[22:40] Rafael Mendes: On success definition: for streaming, success is “delivered at least one token and ended normally.” Failure is “no token and disconnect/timeout” or “server error mid-stream.”

[22:56] Nadia Rahman: And we should record “bytes sent” or “tokens sent” so we can tell if it died after 1 token.

[23:03] Amara Diallo: That’s possible. We emit an event per chunk maybe.

[23:10] Sean Gallagher: Ok. Let’s do a quick round of risks.

[23:14] Priya Natarajan: Risk one: metrics cardinality and cost. We need to keep model labels constrained. Maybe only top N models or group into model families.

[23:26] Logan Wright: Risk two: data correctness. Especially streaming. We need validation queries to compare logs vs metrics.

[23:34] Lauren Bishop: Risk three: Dedicated readiness definition becoming an endless debate. We need a pragmatic v1.

[23:44] Connor O'Brien: Risk four: gates blocking urgent fixes. We need a clear override process and “warn-only” first.

[23:52] Marissa Cole: Risk five: customer interpretation. Even if this is internal first, support will start quoting SLOs. We need language.

[24:02] Sean Gallagher: Great list.

[24:05] Talia Benson: We’re at ~24 minutes in. Do we want to spend remaining time on the open questions list.

[24:12] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Open questions:
1) Streaming disconnect attribution.
2) TTFT thresholds.
3) Dedicated readiness SLI definition.
4) Which services are in the pilot for gates.
5) Whether 429 counts.

[24:28] Paula Mendes: For pilot services, I suggest API gateway and routing control plane. They’re central and already have canary workflows.

[24:36] Ethan Park: Control plane yes, but we need to make sure it’s not blocking itself. Like, if control plane budget is exhausted, how do we deploy the fix.

[24:46] Connor O'Brien: Overrides. And “break glass” for incident fixes.

[24:52] Aisha Bello: Also, we can scope gating to the specific tier. If Hosted is burning but Dedicated isn’t, you can still deploy Dedicated-only changes.

[25:02] Jordan Lee: That requires tier-aware scoping in policy engine.

[25:06] Priya Natarajan: Which is the whole point.

[25:09] Mina Haddad: On 429, I think we should treat protective throttling as a separate SLI and show it in Console. Even if excluded from availability, customers will see it.

[25:22] Marissa Cole: Agree. We can name it “throttled responses rate.”

[25:27] Sean Gallagher: Good.

[25:30] Rafael Mendes: TTFT thresholds: we should pick a threshold per tier. Hosted maybe looser, Dedicated tighter. But it’s model-dependent.

[25:40] Nadia Rahman: That’s why we might do TTFT SLO as percentile, not absolute threshold.

[25:46] Aisha Bello: We can do p95 TTFT < X seconds for a given route group and model family.

[25:55] Priya Natarajan: Model family label is better than exact model string, for cardinality.

[26:02] Logan Wright: But the catalog changes. Need a mapping table.

[26:07] Sergio Costa: For dashboards, we can filter by “model_group.”

[26:11] Sean Gallagher: Ok.

[26:13] Lauren Bishop: Dedicated readiness: I want v1 to be “percent of minutes with baseline capacity available.” Baseline means committed GPUs or tokens/sec. We can measure “healthy replicas >= baseline.”

[26:29] Ethan Park: We can measure healthy replicas easily. Mapping to tokens/sec is harder.

[26:35] Priya Natarajan: Start with replicas/capacity units. That’s v1.

[26:40] Sean Gallagher: Great. We’ll ask Vanessa for proposal.

[26:45] Amara Diallo: For streaming disconnect, I’ll own the inventory. But I need runtime folks to confirm what errors are emitted when upstream dies.

[26:56] Mina Haddad: I can connect you to runtime thread but not on this call.

[27:00] Sean Gallagher: We’ll set a follow-up.

[27:03] Talia Benson: Do we need to talk about documentation deliverables.

[27:07] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Deliverables:
- Confluence page: Tiered SLO definitions, plus exclusions.
- Confluence page: Error budget policy and enforcement.
- A spec for SLIs, like how to compute success/timeouts/disconnects.
- Dashboard and alerting standard.
- ADR for tier-aware enforcement.

[27:31] Marissa Cole: Console MVP spec will follow later, but we need the data model stable.

[27:37] Paula Mendes: For rollouts, we can integrate once budget-check endpoint exists.

[27:43] Ethan Park: We’ll do a minimal endpoint returning: status=green/yellow/red, remaining_budget, burn_rate, and scope.

[27:54] Jordan Lee: And reason codes like “availability burn high” vs “latency burn.”

[28:00] Sergio Costa: That’s useful for alerts too.

[28:04] Sean Gallagher: Ok. Last 10 minutes, we’ll do recap and confirm dates.

[28:10] Sean Gallagher: Aisha drafts Hosted SLO strawman by next Thursday. Lauren provides Dedicated expectations same time. Amara inventories streaming metrics by next Friday. Logan/Nadia look at label/cardinality by end of month. Connor drafts enforcement policy by end of month. Sergio drafts dashboard structure by end of month. Jordan/Ethan propose budget-check API shape in two weeks. Talia sends plan tomorrow.

[28:43] Talia Benson: Yep.

[28:45] Rafael Mendes: And we’ll start building dashboards in parallel with SLI definitions.

[28:50] Sergio Costa: I’ll need access to current Grafana folders to see what exists.

[28:54] Priya Natarajan: We can grant access.

[28:57] Nadia Rahman: One more: we should define what’s out of scope. Like we’re not changing contracts.

[29:03] Sean Gallagher: Correct. This is internal reliability program. Commercial SLA is separate.

[29:10] Lauren Bishop: But support will ask for language to share.

[29:13] Marissa Cole: We can coordinate with docs folks, but initial is internal.

[29:18] Sean Gallagher: Ok.
